Selected projects

Some of the work and projects I've put together, systems built for businesses I support daily, and hands on builds that solve real business challenges.

Finn's Realty

A chatbot that actually knows the business

Real estate offices get the same handful of questions on repeat. Is this unit still available, who's the agent for this area, can someone show me around without a person on site. Finn's Realty was fielding all of that manually, which meant a potential client could message at 9pm and just sit there waiting until morning.

Read the full story

I built them a chatbot that lives inside Telegram and actually knows the business, not a generic script. It pulls from the company's own documents and reads live property data from a spreadsheet, so when someone asks about a listing, the answer is real.

Then I did something most people skip: I tried to break it. I asked it to write me a script to scrape competitor listings, just to see what it would do. It refused and steered the conversation back to Finn's Realty's own properties instead. That mattered to me more than the answers it got right, because a bot that says yes to everything isn't actually useful, it's just agreeable.

SmileCare Dental

Turning website visitors into booked appointments

Picture a dental clinic's website getting steady traffic, people filling out a form for a free consultation, and then silence. No one following up fast enough, no way to see who's actually close to booking versus who filled out a form and forgot about it five minutes later.

Read the full story

That was the gap I closed for SmileCare. I built a funnel page with the offer front and center, connected it to a pipeline that tracks every lead from new contact through to confirmed appointment, and set up an automation that handles the in between part nobody wants to do manually: sending reminders, waiting a set amount of time, then deciding what happens next.

If someone doesn't respond, the system flags it as a cold lead. If they're ready, it notifies the team to confirm the booking. Nothing sits in limbo.

Koka Shortlet

Turning five channels of chaos into one system

Twelve properties is already a lot to keep straight. Twelve properties spread across two countries, with maintenance issues reported over WhatsApp, email, Airbnb messages, Booking.com, and random spreadsheets, is close to chaos. That was the situation at Koka Shortlet before I stepped in.

Read the full story

My job was to take that mess and turn it into something one person could actually manage. I built three connected boards covering maintenance, guest experience, and procurement, so a broken toaster reported in a guest review and a replacement part ordered from Amazon show up as the same story instead of two disconnected facts nobody links together. I took twenty five real, messy, scattered issues and organized every single one of them into the system as a working example.

Then I layered automations on top: a damage report automatically creates a purchase task, assignees get matched by role instead of someone guessing who's free, and a dashboard on top gives whoever's in charge a live read on cost, workload, and which flats keep causing problems.

PharmaCO

A tracker simple enough for a non technical team

Change management in a pharmaceutical company sounds dry until you realize what's actually riding on it. One supplier notification, one small process change, can trigger a chain of assessments, sign offs, and meetings, and if a single piece of that chain gets dropped, that's a real problem for a regulated company.

Read the full story

The team I built this for wasn't technical and didn't want to become technical, they just needed a tracker that told them five things clearly: what's pending, who owns it, what's overdue, what's blocked, and what's ready to close. So I built exactly that in Airtable.

Every change starts as an intake record, flows into a full change record, and spins off whatever child tasks it needs, assessments, action items, follow ups, without anyone re-typing information twice. Formulas calculate how many days are left automatically, and the system sends a reminder before something becomes overdue instead of after, which is the whole point.

Meridian Properties

Two systems that catch what people miss

Meridian was running a property management operation the hard way. Vendor invoices arrived by email and got processed by hand, maintenance tickets lived on a spreadsheet that only worked if everyone remembered to update it, and there was no real connection between the two.

Read the full story

I built two systems that talk to each other. The first takes every invoice submitted through a form and checks it against a list of approved vendors and known properties. If everything matches, it gets approved and posted for review. If something's off, a vendor that isn't approved, a property code that doesn't exist, a duplicate invoice number, it gets pulled into an exception queue instead of quietly causing a problem later.

The second system runs on its own clock, checking every open maintenance ticket once an hour and escalating the ones that have been sitting too long, based on how urgent they are. It even remembers what it's already sent, so nobody gets the same alert five times in a row. And the two systems aren't separate: if an invoice gets flagged because the vendor isn't approved, that automatically creates a ticket for someone to actually go look at it.
